entries.title: CPS wins back millions in federal funding after Trump administration settles lawsuit
entries.summary: <p>Chicago Public Schools has won back millions of dollars in federal grants that top education officials took away after concluding that the school district had violated students’ civil rights by having a Black Student Success Plan and policies that support transgender students.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://clearinghouse.net/case/47906/" target="_blank" ><u>CPS sued the federal government in March</u></a> alleging that the grants were taken away without following the process required by law. That case was settled on Thursday after the U.S. Department of Education agreed to return the funds by Friday, according to a court document dismissing the case.</p><p>CPS officials did not say how much money they expected to be released as part of the settlement. But when the Education Department announced last year that it was stripping the grant, it said it would withhold about $6 million, as well as funding for future years.</p><p>“The District looks forward to working with the U.S. Department of Education to ensure these resources reach schools and students as quickly as possible,” a CPS spokesperson wrote in an email Friday.</p><p>Though it’s a relatively small amount compared to CPS’ $10 billion budget, the settlement reverses the most tangible action taken by the Trump administration against CPS. It is one of several efforts by the Trump administration to force school districts to roll back civil rights and Title IX protections against sex-based discrimination, especially as they pertain to transgender students.</p><p>The Education Department did not respond to questions about why it settled the case.</p><p>CPS officials and board members have refused to back down from their policies, though they have tried not to pick a public fight over them. CPS did not publicly announce that it was suing the federal government or that the case was settled, a fact that was <a class="Link" href="https://news.bloomberglaw.com/litigation/education-department-settles-suit-over-chicago-school-grant-cuts" target="_blank" ><u>first reported by Bloomberg Law</u></a>.</p><p>Since Trump returned to office in 2025, the Education Department and Congress have launched multiple investigations and reviews of CPS policies and spending. As recently as this week, the Republican-led U.S. House Committee on Education and the Workforce <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/08/27/house-education-committee-reviewing-whether-cps-policies-that-support-transgender-students-violate-federal-law" target="_blank" ><u>demanded that CPS send policies and complaints</u></a> as the committee continues to review whether CPS’ protections for transgender students should prompt changes to federal law.</p><p>Education Department officials contend that having a plan that endeavors to improve academic outcomes for Black students harms white and Asian students and educators.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/09/17/feds-threaten-cps-magnet-school-grants-over-black-student-success-plan-treatment-of-trans-students" target="_blank" ><u>In a 2025 letter to CPS</u></a>, Craig Trainor, the acting assistant secretary for civil rights at the time, called the plan “textbook racial discrimination.” He went on to say “no justification proffered by CPS can overcome the patent illegality of its racially exclusionary plan.”</p><p>In that letter, he demanded that CPS abolish the plan.</p><p>He also attacked CPS policies that allow transgender students to play sports and use locker rooms and restrooms that correspond with their gender identity. Trainor wrote in the 2025 letter that those policies are “facially discriminatory on the basis of sex.”</p><p>In CPS’ lawsuit over the loss of the grant, the district contends that it has fully cooperated with the Office for Civil Rights’ investigation into these policies. Yet despite its compliance and the fact that reviews of these policies went away, the Education Department took away the grant.</p><p>The grants are to support some of CPS’ specialized magnet programs. In the lawsuit, CPS points out that the grant specifically went to personalized learning programs and science, engineering and technology classes in high-need schools.</p><p>Without the federal money, CPS had to find other money to cover staff salaries and use contingency funding to continue after-school programs. The “abrupt discontinuation” of the grants “without notice, hearing opportunity or any semblance of due process, significantly undermines the work that CPS engaged in for over 10 years in developing high quality programs,” the lawsuit states.</p><p>CPS officials said they planned to use the returned grant funding “to support continued, high-quality magnet school programming,” though the amount that will be available for this school year is still being determined.</p>

entries.title: Suburban Cook County reports first 4 West Nile virus cases of 2026
entries.summary: <p>The Cook County Department of Public Health has reported the first four cases of West Nile virus in suburban Cook County this year and is urging residents to take precautions against mosquito bites.</p><p>All four cases were identified in adults, the health department said Friday.</p><p>Dr. Kiran Joshi, chief operating officer of Cook County Department of Public Health, urged residents to take steps to protect themselves from mosquitoes.</p><p>“Using insect repellent, wearing long sleeves and pants, and eliminating standing water around your home can help protect you from mosquito bites,” Joshi said in a news release.</p><p>West Nile virus occurs in humans when they are bitten by mosquitoes that contracted the virus from infected birds.</p><p>As of the week ending Aug. 22, the risk of human West Nile virus infection is considered high, the department said.</p><h3>West Nile virus in Illinois</h3><p>The Illinois Department of Public Health on Wednesday reported the state’s first human case of West Nile virus in Piatt County.</p><p>Mosquitoes carrying the virus were <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/06/12/first-west-nile-virus-cases-of-the-year-reported-in-mosquitoes-in-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>reported</u></a> in Illinois in May, but no human cases had been reported at the time.</p><p>Suburban Cook County reported  four deaths related to the virus in 2025, with 44 total cases reported last year, according to the department.</p><p>Instances of West Nile virus increased significantly in 2025 across Illinois compared to 2024, according to the department.</p><p>The state reported 150 confirmed human cases of the virus in 2025, more than doubling the 69 cases reported in 2024. Ten deaths were reported in 2025, compared with 13 deaths the year before. </p><p>Health officials warned that many people infected with West Nile virus have no symptoms and do not become ill. </p><p>Some may develop mild symptoms like fever, headache, rash, and body aches within three to 15 days after infection.</p><p>More severe symptoms can be neuroinvasive, impacting the nervous system, the brain or spinal cord. These symptoms can include high fever, stiff neck, confusion, muscle weakness, and inflammation of the brain, which can cause permanent neurological damage or death. </p><p>In June, CCDPH launched its annual “Fight the Bite” public awareness campaign to encourage residents to take precautions against West Nile virus.</p><h3>How to prevent West Nile virus infection</h3><p>The campaign encourages simple steps to reduce the risk of West Nile virus infection.</p><p>People are encouraged to use EPA-registered insect repellents to ward off the bugs.</p><p>Adults should use repellents containing 20% to 50% DEET, the department said. Child-friendly repellents containing 20% to 30% DEET are recommended for children. </p><p>Residents should also eliminate standing water from flowerpots, old tires, buckets, birdbaths and plastic wading pools where mosquitoes can breed.</p><p>Damaged windows and door screens can also let mosquitoes in. The health department urged people to check that their door and window screens fit tightly and do not have holes or gaps to protect indoor spaces.</p><p> Residents are also reminded to take caution and consider limiting outdoor activities at dawn and dusk when possible as mosquito activity is heightened during these hours. </p><p>To learn more about West Nile virus prevention, visit <a class="Link" href="http://fightthebitecookcounty.com" target="_blank" ><u>FightTheBiteCookCounty.com</u></a>.</p>

entries.title: Davis Martin eyes return to rotation, and first-half form, for home stretch of White Sox’ playoff push
entries.summary: <p>MINNEAPOLIS — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a> starter Davis Martin was relegated to watching his teammates from afar while nursing a blister on the middle finger that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/14/white-sox-put-davis-martin-on-injured-list-call-up-jose-urquidy" target="_blank" ><u>has sidelined him</u></a> for two weeks.</p><p>Suffice to say he’s happy to be watching from the dugout this weekend in Minneapolis, and he’ll be thrilled to be back on the mound next week in Houston.</p><p>“It's huge,” Martin said after rejoining the team Friday following a quick, sharp Triple-A rehab assignment. “I told my wife after just one day in Charlotte, I was just like, ‘I miss my guys. I'm seeing [Tristan Peters] hit <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/26/tristan-peters-white-sox-munetaka-murakami-colson-montgomery-franchise-record-frank-thomas-paul-konerko-carlos-lee-will-venable" target="_blank" ><u>his fifth home run</u></a>.’ I had, like, the super FOMO as I was sitting in my hotel room by myself in Charlotte. I miss my guys, I miss my team, I miss all that. I just want to be back.”</p><p>With a pitching staff gasping toward the finish line in the heat of a pennant race, the Sox are missing Martin just as much — especially the version of Martin they got over the first few months of the season, when their longest-tenured player’s breakout put him in All-Star consideration.</p><p>But it’s been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/04/davis-martin-chicago-white-sox-boston-red-sox-joey-bart-caleb-durbin-edgar-quero-roch-cholowsky" target="_blank" ><u>a slog since late June</u></a> for Martin, whose ERA ballooned to 4.32 before the blister did on his throwing hand.</p><p>At this stage, the Sox will take just about anything they can get from Martin, a week removed from their last game with anyone in the rotation clearing five innings and flagging reliability in starters not named Sean Burke or <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/19/white-sox-rotation-anthony-kay-davis-martin-erick-fedde-will-venable-noah-schultz-jose-urquidy-kyle-teel-zach-bove-cameron-johnson" target="_blank" ><u>Anthony Kay</u></a>.</p><p>The need was made all the more apparent early in the Sox' series opener at Target Field, where the Twins roughed up trade-deadline acquisition Luis Castillo for four runs on seven hits over the first three innings. Sox hitters have done their part to pick up the slack. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Colson Montgomery sent that one outta here! 🚀 <a href="https://t.co/h7gcDIT2Hb">pic.twitter.com/h7gcDIT2Hb</a></p>— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) <a href="https://x.com/whitesox/status/2093495551333474607?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 29, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Martin evoked his first-half form with five innings of scoreless, one-hit ball on Thursday for the Knights, walking one and fanning five while throwing 40 of his 59 pitches for strikes.</p><p>The 29-year-old right-hander often looked unhittable over the first two-plus months of the season, but has labored to a 6.52 ERA over his last 15 starts. His IL stint was as valuable for physical recovery as it was mental.</p><p>“It was a good time to mentally reset,” he said. “Good time to really just focus in on bullpens, be able to actually get stuff out of bullpens because you are fresher than just your normal Day Two ‘pen after throwing 100 pitches so you're able to work on stuff, you're able to really dive into a lot of these things, and I think we did a really good job of refining all that stuff, and I think mentally, we're in a really good spot.”</p><p>With Martin lined up to start Tuesday but not yet officially penciled in, manager Will Venable called it “really important to get him back and healthy and [to] kind of stabilize our rotation.”</p><p>“He's been one of our guys in the middle of everything all year,” Venable said. “Obviously, we know that when he's right, what he's capable of doing, he's been as valuable as any player. So to have him back, and get that type of player back, that guy that's a leader in our clubhouse in every way possible — he makes an impact on our club.”</p><p>The timing is not lost on Venable, whose squad has four more key division series over the final month of the season.</p><p>“They're going to decide it all,” the second-year manager said. “It’s what it's all about, being able to take care of your own division. And in our case, every one of these clubs in our division are really good.”</p><p>And Martin wouldn’t miss it for the world.</p><p>“It's everything that we worked for,” he said. “We had a few team meetings last year basically saying, ‘Hey, if you don't believe that we can do this, like, you don't need to be in this room.’ And a lot of guys that were on that team are still here and still ready to roll and still pushing… Now it's just time to finish. It's time to empty the tank and give it everything we got.”</p>

entries.title: Standing-room-only crowd watches DePaul Prep beat Lane in a showdown of North Side neighbors
entries.summary: <p>Two schools separated by a few hundred feet met for the first time in almost four decades before a standing-room-only crowd on Friday night.</p><p>The game was worth the wait.</p><p>DePaul Prep's defense stopped a Lane run at the one-yard line as time ran out, sealing a 6-0 home win for the Rams.</p><p>The last time the teams played, it was 1989, DePaul was known as Gordon Tech and its campus was a half-mile west at Addison and California.</p><p>Neither head coach and obviously none of the players had seen the rivalry firsthand before. But now that they have, they're looking forward to its renewal next year at Lane's bigger stadium.</p><p>"It was a great atmosphere,' DePaul Prep linebacker Julian Stump said. "Seeing them across the street every day, there's just something different about it. And knowing that you're now going to have that built[-in] rivalry with those people and have to play them in the future, it's definitely special."</p><p>"Obviously the geography speaks for itself," first-year DePaul Prep coach Nick Bizzieri said. "Tonight was a lot of fun. There was a lot of juice in the air. I wish the show could have been better on both sides, but I hope this is something we can keep going. I would love to do this every year."</p><p>So would Lane coach Deshon Conley.</p><p>"There was a lot of energy in the stadium," he said. "It was fun, for sure."</p><p>The game's only score came in the final minute of the third quarter when DePaul sophomore quarterback Andrew Campbell found a seam on the right side and ran for a four-yard TD.</p><p>"The previous two plays, I saw the D-end crashing in on those runs," Campbell said. "I told myself before that play, I have to pull this one. And I pulled it out and I ran right in."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b60000" name="image-b60000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d1ddad2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3529x1981+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F33%2F42%2F70ea8c5c482f8a0d5b35f17f2ad4%2Fmc-cst-082926-007.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ab92cda/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3529x1981+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F33%2F42%2F70ea8c5c482f8a0d5b35f17f2ad4%2Fmc-cst-082926-007.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7be8415/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3529x1981+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F33%2F42%2F70ea8c5c482f8a0d5b35f17f2ad4%2Fmc-cst-082926-007.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="DePaul Prep's Zach Stewart (4) carries the ball against Lane. "He goes inside, I go outside, so it opened up a perfect lane for me."</p><p>A 20-yard pass from Blake Perkins to Shamar Pipes got the ball to the four, but Lane couldn't score on two runs and time ran out. D'Angelo Bell ran for 70 yards for Lane (1-1) and Pipes rushed for 68.</p><p>DePaul is 2-0 after an eventful offseason. Former coach Mike Passarella left for a college job, Bizzieri was promoted in May and more than 10 players transferred out.</p><p>"We're just a whole bunch of hungry kids putting everything together with each other," Campbell said. "We're the definition of family out there."</p>

The Caravan didn’t roll over Oswego; they had to fight for the title.</p><p>There is still a major gap in perception between the two programs. entries.title: Dear Abby: Retired Husband Drives Remote Worker Wife Up a Wall
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am at my wits' end with "Barney," my husband of 35 years. He retired two years ago, but I am still working and likely will for several more years. I've worked from home successfully since long before the COVID-19 pandemic, which was fine while Barney was working. When he retired, I talked to him about respecting boundaries during the day while I work. My home office is on the second floor of the house, which leaves him the entire downstairs to enjoy without disrupting me during work hours.</p><p>Unfortunately, Barney has not shown me the respect I asked for. He frequently yells upstairs for me to come help him with something, or he comes into the office and wants to talk. He wants to know what's for dinner, and he gets upset if I'm not done working at exactly 5 p.m. He also gets upset with me if I won't let him caress and hold me while I'm trying to work. When he worked, he often stayed late and went in after hours or on weekends. I never complained or showed him the disrespect he is showing me.</p><p>For a while, I tried to give Barney more attention because I do love him. Now, his constant complaining is so annoying that I don't even want to spend my free time with him. I am certainly not interested in any physical expressions of love. I've tried to discuss this with him and even asked if he'd consider going to couples counseling, but he refuses.</p><p>I'm a happy woman except when I'm with my husband. That makes me sad, and I'm tired of feeling this way. I'm not sure what to do. I've thought about renting office space, but that would only solve the disruption issues during my workday. It wouldn't solve the other issues, notably Barney's lack of respect for me. — <i>GIVE ME SPACE</i></p><p><b>DEAR GIVE ME SPACE:</b> A partial solution is better than no solution. Go ahead and rent the office space. It will be helpful to learn how much of the pressure that relieves. Once your work frustrations are out of the picture, reassess Barney's treatment of you and decide how much relationship adjustment is still needed. Even if he refuses counseling, go by yourself! If you do, you may learn some techniques for dealing with his troublesome behaviors.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My 40-year-old niece has lived in my sister's basement for five years now. She has had many ups and downs since running away at 15, but she was able to get a degree in engineering, fly helicopters, etc., so she is intelligent. I don't know why she has withdrawn to such a degree.</p><p>Should I ask my sister or brother-in-law how she is doing when I call? I feel it's normal and natural that I ask, but the question always brings a painful silence followed by, "She's figuring out her life." She does not work or look for it, hides from the public, and behaves like a 16-year-old. Should I quit asking? — <i>UNCLE IN THE DARK</i></p><p><b>DEAR UNCLE:</b> If you do not ask how your niece is doing, it will appear that you do not care. So, the next time you speak to your relatives and your question is met with an uncomfortable pause, consider asking whether they would rather you not ask.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned the column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: Postal Service is supposed to deliver mail, not decide who gets to vote
entries.summary: <p>The founders of our democracy understood a simple truth: No president should wield unchecked power over the machinery of elections.</p><p>That principle is embedded throughout our Constitution. Congress, not the White House, established the U.S. Postal Service. States and Congress, not the president, set the rules for federal elections. Our system depends on independent institutions that serve the public equally rather than advancing the interests of those who temporarily hold political power.</p><p>Today, that constitutional principle is under assault.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-fb0000" name="module-fb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>A federal judge last week <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/08/26/nx-s1-5945260/trump-mail-in-voting-ballots" target="_blank" >lifted a nationwide injunction </a>that had blocked the Postal Service from implementing portions of President Donald Trump's executive order restricting mail-in voting, potentially transforming Postal Service from a neutral carrier of ballots into a gatekeeper of voting rights.</p><p>The ruling did not address the constitutionality of the administration's directive requiring states to provide absentee voter lists to the Postal Service, which would then determine how ballots are processed and delivered. </p><p>Instead, it cleared a procedural hurdle while broader legal challenges continue. At issue is a fundamental constitutional question: whether a president can use an independent federal institution to exercise powers over elections that the Constitution assigns to Congress and the states.</p><p>The Postal Service was deliberately structured to operate independently of the White House. Following postal reforms enacted in 1970, Congress insulated the agency from direct presidential control, placing it under an independent Board of Governors and assigning it a clear mission: provide universal service to the American people regardless of geography, income or political affiliation.</p><p>Yet Trump has repeatedly proposed bringing the Postal Service under the control of the Commerce Department and has entertained broader efforts to weaken or eliminate its independent governance structure. Reports earlier this year indicated that administration officials were exploring ways to place the Postal Service under direct executive branch authority, a move that legal scholars and postal experts warned could violate the framework Congress established to protect the agency from political manipulation.</p><p>The Postal Service exists to deliver ballots, not determine who should receive them.</p><p>It exists to serve the people, not police voters.</p><p>It exists to facilitate democratic participation, not stand in the way of it.</p><p>When an administration seeks greater control over election infrastructure while simultaneously claiming authority to determine voter eligibility, Americans should ask not only whether those actions are legal but whether they honor the democratic values our institutions were created to protect.</p><p>The implications extend beyond elections. The Postal Service delivers prescription drugs to seniors, benefits checks to retirees, correspondence to military families and business shipments to every corner of the nation. More than 600,000 postal workers sustain a universal service network that reaches addresses no private carrier would willingly serve. Access to that network should never depend upon loyalty to the party in power.</p><p>Last week's court ruling makes this debate more urgent. The administration has already succeeded, at least temporarily, in clearing the way for a trusted public institution to be used as a vehicle for expanding presidential control over elections. The Constitution deliberately disperses power over voting to prevent exactly this kind of partisan manipulation.</p><p>The National Urban League has long defended voting rights, democratic participation and the integrity of public institutions. We believe the Postal Service should remain independent, nonpartisan and accountable to the American people, not to the political agenda of any administration.</p><p>As thousands gathered Friday for the <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-live-march-on-washington-rally-draws-attention-to-voting-rights-with-jeffries-sanders" target="_blank" >March on Washington: Defend the Vote </a>rally, they stood in the shadow of the Lincoln Memorial, where the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. reminded the nation that democracy requires constant vigilance. Sixty-three years later, the struggle is not only about access to the ballot box but about protecting the institutions that make free and fair elections possible. When independent public institutions are drawn into partisan battles over voting rights, Americans of every political persuasion should recognize what is at stake: the integrity of our democracy itself.</p><p>The mail belongs to the people.</p><p>The ballot belongs to the voter.</p><p>The institution entrusted with delivering both should never be weaponized for partisan gain.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/marc-h-morial" target="_blank" ><i>Marc H. Morial</i></a><i> is president and CEO of the National Urban League</i> <i>and</i> <i>was mayor of New Orleans from 1994 to 2002.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-840000" name="module-840000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Loop company's bid to buy Arizona bank would spike predatory lending, consumer advocacy groups argue
entries.summary: <p>Consumer advocacy groups and the state’s top law enforcement official are opposing a Chicago company’s plan to obtain a national bank charter — arguing the move would allow it to lock customers into loans at more than 100% interest rate. </p><p>Their ire is directed at online lender and servicer Opportunity Financial, which is seeking regulatory approvals for a $130 million deal to acquire BNCCORP and its subsidiary BNC National Bank, a nationally chartered commercial bank in Arizona. </p><p>If approved, OppFi would be able to evade state laws that cap interest rates for borrowers. </p><p>Illinois has a 36% interest rate cap on consumer loans and is among 45 states that impose a rate limit, according to the National Consumer Law Center.</p><p>“Largely, banks and credit unions are not the problem in the predatory lending space,” said Jane Doyle, director of policy and advocacy for the Woodstock Institute, a Chicago nonprofit that advocates for consumer protections. “The problem comes in when companies like OppFi try to get their own banking charter to get around that exemption.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-920000" name="html-embed-module-920000"></a><div style="min-height:417px" id="datawrapper-vis-okOme"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/okOme/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-okOme"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/okOme/full.png" alt="Maximum APRs for six‑month, $500 installment loan (Choropleth map)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Federal banking rules allow banks with national charters to levy the maximum interest rates established in their home state to borrowers in states with stricter laws or lower caps. So online companies like OppFi are able to skirt state caps by partnering with charter banks in states like Utah that lack interest rate caps — partnerships described as a "rent-a-bank" scheme by industry critics.</p><p>Meanwhile, borrowers of the high interest loans often end up paying double or triple the principal, pushing them further into debt. Studies show these loans disproportionately affect Black and Latino communities. And lax federal regulations and the dismantling of consumer protections by the Trump administration is making these loans more pervasive, evident by a surge of fintech companies and other digital platforms applying for national bank charters, like Loop-based Enova International.</p><p>Enova is expected to close its $369 million purchase of New York-based Grasshopper Bancorp and its online bank subsidiary during the second half of the year — a deal that has also drawn opposition from consumer advocacy groups and attorneys general.</p><p>OppFi confirmed plans to relocate its headquarters from 130 E. Randolph St. to Utah, following its acquisition of BNCCORP. The cash and stock transaction, expected to close in the fourth quarter, requires regulatory approval from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, Federal Reserve Board and Federal Deposit Insurance Corp.</p><h3>Opposition mounts</h3><p>Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul and 17 other state attorneys general sent a letter on Aug. 6 to the OCC, Federal Reserve and FDIC urging the agencies to deny OppFi’s pending acquisition. </p><p>“OppFi should not be granted a national bank charter because it targets vulnerable consumers with risky, unsafe and unsound loans that cause more financial harm,” Raoul said.</p><p>They argued OppFi's acquisition would increase "unaffordable high-cost loans” that pose significant safety concerns for consumers, small businesses and the banking system while allowing the company to circumvent state laws protecting borrowers. A similar letter about Enova, signed by 15 state attorneys general, including Raoul, was written in July.</p><p>“It’s unfortunate that a group of politically motivated AGs chose to issue a poorly researched letter that is unsupported by the facts, attacking companies focused on providing credit access,” OppFi said in a statement. “OppFi's mission is to expand access to credit for hardworking consumers who are overlooked by traditional financial institutions.”</p><p>The company markets personal and small business loans to help consumers cover emergencies, medical bills, debt consolidation and large purchases, among other expenses. OppFi’s available market includes 48 million Americans and 12 million small businesses lacking traditional credit options, according to its website.</p><p>“They’re not writing $500,000 mortgages,” Dave Storms, director of equity research at Dallas-based Stonegate Capital Partners, said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-d90000" name="image-d90000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/eb155d9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7826x4392+0+828/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F35%2F9a%2F81cb42594f90b3a6a914aa36a698%2Foppfi-260830-02.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/799b4f6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7826x4392+0+828/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F35%2F9a%2F81cb42594f90b3a6a914aa36a698%2Foppfi-260830-02.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9096f73/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7826x4392+0+828/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F35%2F9a%2F81cb42594f90b3a6a914aa36a698%2Foppfi-260830-02.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Outside OppFi's headquarters at 130 E. Randolph St. in the Loop." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9096f73/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7826x4392+0+828/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F35%2F9a%2F81cb42594f90b3a6a914aa36a698%2Foppfi-260830-02.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6a9a7c9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7826x4392+0+828/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F35%2F9a%2F81cb42594f90b3a6a914aa36a698%2Foppfi-260830-02.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9096f73/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7826x4392+0+828/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F35%2F9a%2F81cb42594f90b3a6a914aa36a698%2Foppfi-260830-02.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Outside OppFi’s headquarters at 130 E. Randolph St. in the Loop.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Storms said their business is predicated on volume, with most loans around $1,000.</p><p>OppFi said every applicant is evaluated on income and cash flow to verify their ability to repay.</p><p>But its customers are struggling to pay them back, according to financial filings and customer accounts.</p><p>OppFi reported 52.3% of its outstanding loan balances on an annualized basis were charged off in the second quarter due to delinquencies, personal bankruptcies or other reasons deemed uncollectible. An annualized charge-off rate is a proportion of total loans deemed uncollectible, with the creditor typically writing it off as bad debt after 90 days of missed payments.</p><p>OppFi said evaluating short-term credit using its annualized charge-off metrics is misleading. </p><p>“The true measure of repayment health is lifetime charge-off rate, which holds steady within our historical baseline of 20% to 25%,” the company said.</p><p>Still, the recently reported charge-off rate was higher than analysts expected, according to Storms, who covers the company.</p><p>“One data point doesn't make a trend but certainly something to monitor,” he said.</p><h3>‘Repairing my life’</h3><p>Facing mounting bills and a new mortgage payment on a house she inherited after her parents died, Courtney Thompson turned to OppFi to fill the gap. She went through the quick approval process in 2024, borrowing $3,000.</p><p>In September 2025, she stopped making the monthly $124.17 repayments. A month later, the loan was written off.</p><p>“I did the best that I could to stay afloat,” the 40-year-old South Holland single mother of three said. “After a while, I got behind.”</p><p>Providing for her family and juggling monthly bills, as well as her parents funeral costs took precedence.</p><p>“I communicated with OppFi and let them know what was going on,” she said. “They didn't care. They wanted their money.”</p><p>If Thompson paid back the $3,000 loan with its 127.6% APR over two years, as the contract stipulated, the total balance would have skyrocketed to $6,829.35.</p><p>The first time she used OppFi, following a coworker's recommendation, was in 2021, when she borrowed $1,600 to cover bills and gifts for the holidays. She paid it back in about 18 months, with the final balance exceeding $3,500.</p><p>“You're not realizing how much you pay back,” she said. “I wish there were better loan options out there.”</p><div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Sisters Kesha Thompson-Warren and Courtney Thompson each took out loans through OppFi and faced an interest rate of more than 100%.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jeremy Battle/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>When Thompson’s sister, Kesha Thompson-Warren, 44, took out a loan with OppFi in 2023 her interest rate was 159.5%. </p><p>Thompson-Warren, a mother of two who lives in South Holland, said the loan, which required garnishing her income, helped cover a variety of bills, including expenses for her landscaping business, mortgage payments and funeral costs for her parents, who both lacked life insurance policies.</p><p>“I took out maybe $1,000 and ended up paying double or triple that,” she said. “I'm still repairing my life after all the interest I had to deal with. I just feel taken advantage of.”</p><p>OppFi said it rejects claims that its business model creates a cycle of debt.</p><p>“OppFi facilitates fully amortizing, fixed-term installment loans with clear repayment schedules and zero prepayment penalties,” the company said. “In fact, one-third of customers use loans originated through our platform to pay off higher-cost alternatives like payday loans.”</p><h3>Legal limits</h3><p>Illinois lawmakers in 2021 passed the Predatory Loan Prevention Act, which capped interest rates on most consumer loans at 36%. The bill was meant to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/consumer-affairs/2024/03/14/payday-lenders-illinois-residents-loans-interest-rate-cap-woodstock" >combat payday lenders</a> that, unlike fintech companies such as OppFi, require customers to repay on their next payday.</p><p>Even though payday lenders have left the state, Woodstock said there are still lenders who are evading state law by partnering with banks in states with no rate caps.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-bf0000" name="html-embed-module-bf0000"></a><div style="min-height:417px" id="datawrapper-vis-3ulqZ"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/3ulqZ/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-3ulqZ"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/3ulqZ/full.png" alt="Maximum APRs for two‑year, $2,000 installment loan (Choropleth map)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Given the proprietary nature of OppFi’s business and its bank partnership agreements, it’s difficult pinpointing the number of loans it facilitates annually or the interest rates attached to them, but a national research study and some lawsuits offer insights.</p><p>From 2020 to April 2022, OppFi provided more than 38,000 California consumers with loans carrying principal amounts between $500 and $4,000. The average APR was 153%, according to court documents. In Washington, D.C., it was providing loans to most residents at a 160% APR, according to a 2021 lawsuit. </p><p>A January report from the Center for Responsible Lending found that OppFi facilitated personal installment loans with up to 195% APR on loans ranging from $500 to $5,000.</p><p>Meanwhile, borrowers in the last three years have filed nearly 1,700 complaints against OppFi, according to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.</p><p>“Somebody needs to advocate for us,” said Thompson-Warren, whose story of financial hardship helped push Illinois lawmakers to enact a rate cap.</p><p>She’s still struggling, deferring payments on student loans that exceed $100,000 while trying to build her landscaping business and launch a logistics company. She also works in an administrative role at a South Loop hotel.</p><p>“If I didn't have my business, I would probably drown,” Thompson-Warren said. “So there’s not really a lesson I can tell anybody because this is what we're up against.”</p><p>It's unlikely the federal regulatory landscape will sharply curb the industry's growth.</p><p>Since 2025, the OCC has received 40 new bank charter applications and approved 21, denying only two — many applications are from the fintech and crypto sector. Recently, the regulator granted preliminary approval to World Liberty Financial Trust Co., a cryptocurrency venture affiliated with President Donald Trump and his family.</p><p>From 2021 to 2024, the OCC received only 18 new bank applications and approved half of them. Over the previous decade, there were some years when the agency received no charter applications.</p><p>“This administration definitely in the second term is much more M&A friendly with banks,” said Rob Farling, national risk and regulatory banking lead at West Monroe, a Chicago-based consulting firm that helps banks with mergers and acquisitions.</p><p>That's helped spur M&A activity for non-banks seeking national charters via acquisition, similar to OppFi and Enova.</p><p>“We've definitely seen an uptick,” Farling said. “A lot of people are expecting to see even more in 2027.”</p><p>Meanwhile, Thompson is working overtime to make her mortgage payments but she has already ruled out a high interest loan.</p><p>“It’s so stressful,” she said. “But I would take a different route.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/consumer-affairs/2024/03/14/payday-lenders-illinois-residents-loans-interest-rate-cap-woodstock" >Fewer Illinois residents using payday lenders after state capped interest rates</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Bears coach Ben Johnson is trying to move the team forward by putting it in his players' hands
entries.summary: <p>NASHVILLE, Tenn. — There are a handful of topics guaranteed to irritate <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/01/the-bears-and-their-fans-needed-a-truth-teller-they-got-one-in-new-coach-ben-johnson" target="_blank" >Ben Johnson</a>.</p><p>He doesn’t want to be pressed for updates about injured cornerback Kyler Gordon and doesn’t like inquiries about whether he plans to play quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" target="_blank" >Caleb Williams</a> and the other starters in preseason games, such as the one the Bears will play Saturday against the Titans.</p><p>But he really hates any questions pertaining to last season.</p><p>Why, though, would that bother him? It was a spectacular turnaround for the Bears, who won the NFC North and won their first playoff game in 15 years. Johnson also was a finalist for Coach of the Year.</p><p>‘‘Are you trying to annoy me right now?’’ he replied, glaring with a fury rivaling the scorching Tennessee sun.</p><p>He sees no purpose in looking back. He’s moving forward at full speed. Always.</p><p>‘‘All I care about is, does it help us win or not?’’ Johnson said. ‘‘Talking about last year isn’t going to do us any good in terms of winning . . . the next preseason game, winning Week 1.’’</p><p>Johnson is proud of what he and the team achieved last season and has said so, but his point is on target: This is a new adventure. Even with some carryover on the roster, it’s a new team. And he’s coaching it differently.</p><p>He remains the ultra-competitive, intense, hard-driving coach he always has been, but he hasn’t seen the need to give his team a butt-kicking, as he did last season. He has been talking about his players taking ownership, especially on offense, and him stepping back is part of that.</p><p>When Johnson gets after the team, it’s every bit as fierce as before — ‘‘He’s still extremely sharp and very, very tough,’’ quarterback Caleb Williams said — but those moments have happened less often. In fact, Williams was the one who lost his temper in the joint practice Thursday with the Titans and Johnson who stepped in to say, ‘‘Calm down.’’</p><p>Add it to the list of things he has been teaching Williams, who needs to know every concept and variation in Johnson’s playbook. He needs to be so dialed in to defensive coverages that he’s a step ahead of his opponents when he takes the snap. He needs to straighten out his footwork and throw more accurately. But he also must learn to lead.</p><p>‘‘He’s allowing us players to be able to step up,’’ Williams said when he was asked what Johnson is handling differently this season. ‘‘You win championships when you’re a player-led team, so Coach is trying to allow us to do that, and he steps in whenever he needs to.’’</p><p>Williams has made some headway in that area but still has further to go.</p><p>Everything from the play-call to the snap is smoother than it was a year ago, and that’s the starting point for running Johnson’s offense effectively. Johnson spent much of their first training camp together yelling for Williams to get out of the huddle, but there hasn’t been any of that this time.</p><p>One of the best ways to lead, however, is also to play well. It’s hard for Williams to have credibility unless he shows it on the field. His late-game heroics certainly made him a magnet for teammates, but the truest sign of growth this season will be implementing everything Johnson has been saying.</p><p>Johnson wants Williams to complete 70% of his passes. He wants him to make better reads and not skip past good options early in the play. He wants steadiness, so those last-minute escapes aren’t necessary.</p><p>Once Williams goes from echoing Johnson’s words to transferring them to the way he plays, it’ll be his team. Johnson is trying to get the Bears to that future as fast as he can.</p>

entries.title: What's your favorite monument in Chicago? Here's what you told us
entries.summary: <p>We asked readers what their favorite monument is in Chicago. Here's what you told us, lightly edited for clarity:</p><p>"Haymarket Monument at Randolph and Desplaines streets. It honors the over-50-year struggle to establish the eight-hour day and free speech."<br><i>— Mike Matejka, Normal</i></p><p>"Statue of the Republic in Jackson Park."<br><i>— Dave Pietruszka</i></p><p>"The statue of Alexander Hamilton. It’s not an iconic Chicago monument, but I love how random it is. He’s just down the way a bit from Jefferson, and close to Goethe. I also appreciate the backstory of him being there. It’s so American. I think he’d be pleased. Illinois was barely thought of when Hamilton was killed, but Chicago is very Hamiltonian."<br><i>— Eleanor Shanklin</i></p><p>"The two statues of Native Americans on horses near the east end of I-290. The Bowman and The Spearman (known as the Equestrian Indians). They stand in Congress Plaza at Michigan Avenue and Ida B. Wells Drive, marking the grand entrance to Grant Park."<br><i>— Antonio Cruz</i></p><p>"My favorite monument is the Cook County building at 118 N. Clark St. It is there that President John H. Stroger championed the building of the new Cook County Hospital, a hospital that would serve all those in need of medical attention."<br><i>— Terrence Camodeca</i></p><p>"The lions guarding the Art Institute of Chicago and the Statue of the Republic in Jackson Park. Honorable mention for Buckingham Fountain."<br><i>— Vincenzo Bruno</i></p>

entries.title: Show support for caregivers looking after veterans
entries.summary: <p>My husband Ryan served 12 years with the Army National Guard and made sergeant. The injury came on a training jump: a blow to the head on the way out the door. At 33, doctors identified a rare genetic form of early-onset Alzheimer’s disease, which the injury accelerated. Today at 36, his home is a memory care unit.</p><p>I was carrying our third baby, five months along, as the changes took hold. I set aside my social work job. We sold our house in Florida and resettled in Algonquin near my parents. Three young children, one husband in long-term care, one person coordinating it all.</p><p>I am among the roughly <a class="Link" href="https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA3212-1.html" target="_blank" >14.3 million</a> Americans caring for a wounded, ill or injured service member or veteran. As a 2025 Dole Caregiver fellow with the Elizabeth Dole Foundation, I met many Illinoisans who are in the same boat, facing the same struggles. The proposed omnibus package <a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/9237" target="_blank" >Take Care of America’s Veterans Act</a> would go a long way in helping us.</p><p>Several particular components of the legislation are especially important to my family. The <a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/800" target="_blank" >Precision Brain Health Research Act</a> would fund federal studies of traumatic brain injury and how it connects to dementia and push the Department of Veterans Affairs and Defense Department to share what they find. Ryan may not benefit, but the next soldier who lands wrong might.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2025/12/04/us/video/eric-and-ed-edmundson" target="_blank" >Sharri Briley and Eric Edmundson Veterans Benefits Expansion Act</a> would raise support for the most catastrophically injured veterans and give surviving spouses and children a raise they have not seen in three decades. Many caregivers eventually become survivors. We should not have to choose between paying for care and keeping a home.</p><p>The Veteran Caregiver <a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/879" target="_blank" >Reeducation, Reemployment, and Retirement Act</a> would help caregivers rebuild what caregiving costs us: a job, an income, a retirement.</p><p>Finally, the <a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/2102" target="_blank" >Major Richard Star Act</a> would end the wounded veteran tax that takes earned retirement pay from combat-injured retirees. My household gains nothing from it. Thousands of Illinois veterans do, and I want it passed.</p><p>Sen. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., has spent her career making sure the caregivers, survivors and veterans who came after her are not left to manage alone. We are lucky she is ours. I am asking her, Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., and the rest of our delegation to vote for this bill.</p><p><i>Liana Redshaw, Algonquin</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-120000" name="module-120000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Arts are a moneymaking draw </h3><p>Think back to the last creative experience that moved you: a neighborhood festival, a concert, a museum visit, or even a song playing through your headphones. Now think about how many people helped make that experience possible.</p><p>Art often feels effortless, but behind every creative experience is a vast network of workers, businesses, nonprofits, artists and institutions.</p><p>For me, this work is personal. My daughter has built a career as a professional musician, so I have seen firsthand the dedication, discipline and sacrifice it takes to pursue a life in the arts. I also understand how important it is for artists to have an ecosystem that values their talent and provides opportunities to build sustainable careers.</p><p>New data from <a class="Link" href="https://artsalliance.org/2026/06/arts-alliance-illinois-releases-landmark-2026-study-of-the-chicago-and-illinois-creative-economy/" target="_blank" >Arts Alliance Illinois</a> demonstrates just how important that ecosystem is to our economy.</p><p>Chicago’s creative economy supports more than 212,000 jobs, making it the city’s third-largest industry, surpassing education services, retail and manufacturing. It generates nearly $50 billion annually and contributes $5.7 billion in tax revenue. Statewide, more than 734,000 Illinoisans work in creative industries, generating $148 billion in economic activity.</p><p>The impact reaches far beyond the creative sector. Every dollar generated by Chicago’s creative economy produces an additional 38 cents elsewhere in the local economy. Statewide, that figure rises to 95 cents.</p><p>When someone attends a concert, gallery opening, theater performance or cultural event, they are also supporting restaurants, hotels, transportation and other nearby businesses.</p><p>Yet too many artists and creative workers still earn below a living wage, putting Illinois at risk of losing talent to other states.</p><p>For too long, arts and culture have been treated as recreational or optional. They are neither.</p><p>As a legislator, chair of the House Museums, Arts, Culture and Entertainment Committee, and a member of the Illinois Creative Caucus, I believe this data gives us a powerful tool to advance policies that recognize the creative sector for what it is: essential economic infrastructure.</p><p>Investing in the creative economy means investing in jobs, neighborhoods, tourism, small businesses and Illinois’ competitiveness.</p><p>The creative sector is not a luxury. It is one of the pillars of Chicago’s economy, and it is time we treated it that way.</p><p><i>State Rep. Kimberly Neely du Buclet, D-Chicago</i></p><h3>Chicago flexes its musical muscles</h3><p>Freelancer Graham Meyer's recent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/theater/2026/08/13/broadway-chicago-musical-life-cycle-the-notebook-kevin-mccollum" target="_blank" >piece</a> on Chicago's influential role on musicals was wonderfully detailed and informative. It reminded me of having seen the excellent "Spamalot<i>" </i>in Chicago during its pre-Broadway run. I believe a couple songs were cut from that version before it went to New York. I experienced the same with <a class="Link" href="https://buzzcenterstage.com/theatre/theatre-reviews/item/4927-paradise-square-pre-b-oardway-run-opens.html " target="_blank" >Paradise Square</a>, a musical about the little-known history of an Irish and Black neighborhood in New York prior to the Civil War. Chicagoans were treated to advance viewing, and as Meyer notes, our response shaped the creative design of those shows prior to their New York debuts.</p><p><i>Bill Esler, West Town</i></p><h3>Take preventive steps to save pets </h3><h3></h3><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2025/07/25/pet-owner-surrender-dogs-cats-overwhelming-shelters-rescues" >Owner surrenders</a> at Chicago Animal Care and Control <a class="Link" href="https://news.wttw.com/2025/04/10/chicago-s-city-animal-shelter-faces-overcrowding-owner-surrenders-spike-euthanasia" target="_blank" >jumped 265%</a> last year, with intake climbing past 56 animals a day. The city's other open-admission shelter, the Anti-Cruelty Society, <a class="Link" href="https://blockclubchicago.org/2026/06/26/city-shelter-local-rescues-beyond-capacity-with-cats-and-kitten-season-isnt-over/" target="_blank" >closed its doors</a> to new animals for two weeks in June. It's part of a national pattern.</p><p>Most of us don't think of ourselves as the kind of people who'd surrender our pets, as we consider them family. But a 2025 PetSmart Charities and Gallup study found <a class="Link" href="https://news.gallup.com/poll/659057/pet-owners-skipped-declined-veterinary-care.aspx" target="_blank" >52% of pet owners </a>skipped or declined necessary veterinary care within the year, with 71% citing money as a factor. That's not cruelty. It's what happens when loving an animal like a child collides with today's economics.</p><p>Monthly wellness plans, insurance and preventive care can greatly mitigate these costs.</p><p>I know it personally. I adopted a dog named Shirley, a Weimaraner mix who leaned her whole body against people's legs for attention. Not long after, she got sick with ehrlichiosis, a tick-borne infection that had quietly done damage before we caught it. The animal hospital gave me a number: roughly $25,000 to keep her alive.</p><p>Thankfully, I remembered I had pet insurance (this was before I worked in the industry), and it was the only reason she received the necessary care. They treated her, and we got six more months together before the disease returned. I came home to find her collapsed on the floor. We had about 10 minutes together. She passed peacefully in my arms.</p><p>Monthly tick prevention costs only $25 to $50. It might have saved her.</p><p>The shelters filling up are proof of the gap between how we feel about our pets and what we're able to give them. If you're considering adopting, try fostering first. Encourage friends to adopt. And arm yourself with the right resources, such as wellness visits, vaccines and pet insurance, before the day it suddenly becomes urgent.</p><p>We call them our children. Let's start acting like it. Let's clear the shelters.</p><p><i>Steve Schonberg, New York City </i></p><h3>A raw deal for ‘We the People’</h3><p>Free of charge, We the People provides police to keep Donald Trump safe and secure. Safe and secure, Trump uses police to terrorize, criminalize, disappear, subjugate, suppress, tyrannize, and at times, kill We the People.</p><p>Free of charge, We the People provide Trump with unlimited excellent healthcare. He uses his resulting good health to deny and deprive healthcare and life to We the People.</p><p>It can be said that We the People of the United States democratically elected Trump to be president and try to take good care of him by providing police to keep him safe and unlimited free healthcare to keep him healthy. But he betrays We the People by using his presidency and the good care that We the People provide him by dismantling We the People’s democracy and transforming this democratic U.S. into a dictatorship.</p><p>Ultimately, it can be said that We the People enable and allow Trump to physically, mentally and spiritually abuse, misuse, exploit and tyrannize We the People. In other words, We the People give Trump a good life, and in return Trump gives We the People a bad life and in some cases, death.</p><p><i>Don Buss, Waukegan</i></p><h3>Shame on Trump</h3><p>When I was a schoolboy, we were taught to use the acronym "HOMES" to remind us of the names of the five great lakes: Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie and Superior.  But with the president embarrassingly <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/lake-ontario-canada-america-trump-trade-war-3ac58dca0ca83c15605d4dbff146b28a" target="_blank" >renaming Lake Ontario to Lake America</a>, that word no longer works; we need to switch out the letter "o" with an "a."  I suppose we can use the acronym "SHAME."  Since the vast majority of the lake's surface area and shoreline mileage lie on the Ontario side of the international border, renaming is indeed shameful, making this new acronym very appropriate.</p><p><i>Mike Sinner, West Ridge</i> </p><h3>Kudos to Steinberg’s restraint</h3><p>I commend Neil Steinberg on his discipline and restraint in writing about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/08/25/us-supreme-court-ruling-mail-in-voting-donald-trump-executive-order" >voting being wrecked</a> in a recent column.. When I write about Donald Trump and his coterie, the U.S. Supreme Court and elections, I use lots and lots of dirty words.</p><p><i>Kevin Kann, Libertyville</i></p><h3>O’Hare train plan is off the rails</h3><p>Fifteen minutes from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/08/25/ohare-flyer-train-high-speed-rail-old-post-office" >Downtown to O’Hare Airport</a> by train ? I don't think so.</p><p>When the private backers of this fantasy project appear before City Council, I hope they can keep a straight face. I have dealt with numerous railroads during my career, and there is no way on Earth that you can safely operate a train traveling at grade level, involving three different railroads, with multiple interchanges that can get you from Downtown to O'Hare.</p><p>I assume that the private equity group floating this project also believes in Santa Claus.</p><p><i>Bruce Nathanson, Glenview</i></p><h3>Score one for pettiness </h3><p>As a lifelong Chicago sports fan, I am deeply disappointed by how The Score handled the firing<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/08/21/mike-mulligan-out-as-morning-host-at-the-score-marshall-harris-out-as-midday-host" > of Mike Mulligan</a>. Dropping a 23-year station veteran over the weekend without letting him say a proper on-air goodbye to his loyal audience was completely classless.</p><p>This corporate behavior puts fans like me in an unfair position. I grew up admiring the Payton family legacy and want to support <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/08/23/jarrett-payton-mike-mulligan-the-score-sports-radio-chicago-morning-show-david-haugh-walter-payton" >Jarrett Payton</a> in his new morning role. However, management’s rude treatment of "Mully" makes me question if I want to support this station at all. Instead of enthusiastically telling people that Payton is on morning radio, the conversation now centers on how bogus the station was to a local legend.</p><p>The mature move would be for management to invite Mully back for a final farewell segment to give fans the closure they deserve.</p><p><i>Christopher Collins Sr., Schaumburg</i></p><h3>Ideology shouldn’t trump fair play</h3><p>Questioning whether biological sex matters in athletic competition is often treated as controversial. That strikes me as putting ideology ahead of observable reality.</p><p>If the goal is to persuade the public that gender identity alone should determine participation in every aspect of society, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/wnba/2026/08/12/wnba-task-force-denounces-bad-faith-transgender-debate" >sports is the least </a>convincing place to make that case. Athletic competition exists precisely because physical differences matter. Separate men's and women's divisions were created to ensure fair competition.</p><p>No matter how sincerely someone identifies, biology continues to influence athletic performance. Ignoring that reality won't make it disappear. In the end, facts have a way of asserting themselves, and public policy that denies them is unlikely to endure.</p><p><i>Scott T. Thompson, Bloomington, Indiana</i> </p><h3>Too much basketball drama</h3><p>Is it me, or has the WNBA become the new women’s roller derby, women’s pro wrestling and "Dr. Phil" show?"</p><p><i>John J. Karcz, Lemont</i></p>

entries.title: How we photographed a historic power outage in Gary
entries.summary: <p>This week’s top photo comes from photojournalist and Photo Desk Editor <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/ashlee-rezin" target="_blank" >Ashlee Rezin</a>. Follow her on <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/Ashlee_Rezin" target="_blank" >X</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/ashleerezin/" target="_blank" >Instagram</a>.</p><h3>What makes this photo important?</h3><p>Thousands of residents in Northwest Indiana endured a historic power outage that lasted nearly two weeks after severe storms with 99 mph winds blew through the area on Aug. 11. As a photojournalist, it is my job to tell the story of what life was like for residents of Gary and surrounding communities. I set out to humanize the crisis and give voice to those struggling to make ends meet or feed their children in a world without power.</p><h3>How I got this photo:</h3><p>Melissa Dixon and her family were brave to allow my colleague, reporter Elvia Malagón, and I into their home to tell their story. As the sun continued to set, a neighbor dropped off two plastic containers of spaghetti. Dixon came inside from sitting in her mother's vehicle out front — charging her phone in the car and searching social media for community giveaways — grabbed an LED light and started eating while standing up at her kitchen counter. I backed into a far corner of the kitchen to show that, even with the LED light, the darkness was oppressive and overwhelming.</p><p></p><h3><b>Technical details:</b></h3><ul class="rte2-style-ul" entries.title: Three Bears to watch in Saturday's preseason finale
entries.summary: <p>NASHVILLE, Tenn. — Three players to watch in Saturday night’s preseason finale against the Titans:<br> </p><h3><b>CB Malik Muhammad</b></h3><p>Injuries throughout the position have given the fourth-round rookie ample opportunity to play both outside cornerback and begin to learn the nuances in the slot. The Bears love that he’s a willing tackler. Coach Ben Johnson is excited about the trajectory, though it’s inconsistent: “Going up, little bit down, up,” Johnson said.</p><h3><b>RB Salvon Ahmed</b></h3><p>He’s been the Bears’ second-leading rusher, third-leading receiver and overall yards leader during preseason games. The Bears are trying to see if he’s a special teams fit, though — he played on 37% of kicking downs in Game 1 and 34% in Game 2.</p><p>“He hadn't played a ton in his career, but what is my job? My job and our job … is to develop him to be able to do that,” special teams coordinator Richard Hightower said.</p><h3><b>TE Sam Roush</b></h3><h3></h3><p>He’s locked in as the Bears’ third tight end but is racing the clock to be consistent enough for the Bears to trust Week 1. Johnson said he believes he’ll be “phenomenal” eventually — but Johnson said tight end, behind quarterback, the hardest position to learn, given that they have to learn both passing routes and blocking schemes.</p>

entries.title: Noncitizen voting claims animate Trump's attacks on midterms and set up potential result challenges
entries.summary: <p>The drumbeat by <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/hub/donald-trump" target="_blank" >President Donald Trump</a> and his allies about the perceived threats of voting by people who are not U.S. citizens is getting louder as the November election approaches.</p><p>He is pushing to have the U.S. Postal Service send mail ballots only to <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-mail-voting-supreme-court-157afc3c195ce0a62c522da5ce904b04" target="_blank" >voters verified as U.S. citizens</a>. The Census Bureau promoted <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/fact-check-trump-noncitizen-voting-census-bureau-36cf1524fda629b139b7de5c86119622" target="_blank" >a dubious report</a> about thousands of noncitizens voting in 2020, an election that <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/election-claims-biden-won-explained-bd53b14ce871412b462cb3fe2c563f18" target="_blank" >the Republican lost to Democrat Joe Biden</a>. Trump's <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-elections-mullin-dhs-voter-fraud-save-6871e13d3f0e2caadaf56f9b2bc1580d" target="_blank" >Department of Homeland Security</a> is claiming without providing evidence that 250,000 noncitizens might be on the rolls in just four states.</p><p>This week, the Republican candidate for governor in Maine <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/bobby-charles-audio-ice-polls-maine-governor-4e77e0f06a28d2a8f42b51ce28a91677" target="_blank" >confirmed an audio recording</a> in which he said he plans to ask Trump’s border czar to send U.S. marshals and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to polling places in the state to ensure that only legal voters are casting ballots.</p><p>Evidence of noncitizens voting is continuing to “pile up,” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said when asked about the census report.</p><p>In fact, voting by noncitizens is <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/noncitizens-voting-republicans-election-2024-immigration-09b86e6768f755fd875f3c51b0e8ea70" target="_blank" >extremely rare</a> and is punishable as a felony that carries the potential for deportation. Even so, opponents say the hyperfocus on the issue by Trump and his allies is setting the stage for legal challenges to outcomes he may not like during the midterms in which control of Congress is on the line.</p><p>“Throw out these deceitful, deceptive claims as an excuse for disruptions,” said Alexandra Chandler, director of impact programs, free and fair elections at the nonpartisan Democracy Project. “You can deny the results later.”</p><h4>Census report methodology is flawed, but it could help sow distrust</h4><p>The census report, which the president cited in a Truth Social post, said it found in a “beginning analysis” that 24,000 noncitizens voted illegally in 2020. It cited data from a commercially available voter file, which was checked against federal records.</p><p>Experts say the methodology might have <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/fact-check-trump-noncitizen-voting-census-bureau-36cf1524fda629b139b7de5c86119622" target="_blank" >created false positives</a>. For example, if a person’s name was linked to the wrong address or someone's citizenship status had not been updated in a particular database.</p><p>Details that typically would be included in such a report about error rates were missing, said Justin Levitt, a Loyola Marymount University law professor. Nevertheless, election experts say it could help generate distrust among certain voters during this year’s general election.</p><p>“This is an empty manila folder that the administration will wave around when it says the elections were fraudulent, noncitizens voted,” Levitt said.</p><h4>Election heads puzzled by claim of 250,000 noncitizens on voter rolls</h4><p>Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin's July letter to California, Nevada, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania, alleging that as many as nearly 250,000 noncitizens were registered in those states, was met with skepticism and requests for more information.</p><p>“I have serious doubts about the reliability of your data and accuracy of your claims, since my office has not shared our statewide voter registration list with DHS or any other federal agency or official,” California's secretary of state, Democrat Shirley Weber, said in response.</p><p>In New Jersey, Mullin's department indicated as many as 35,000 noncitizens were registered. Shortly after the letter, the Democratic-controlled state disclosed that about <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/noncitizen-voter-registration-new-jersey-99ef57346bbe09ba2ff606538a76eede" target="_blank" >6,600 noncitizens were improperly registered</a> through its motor vehicle system in 2023 and 2024.</p><p>Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill said those people answered “no” when asked whether they were citizens, but were registered anyway. The governor said her administration found that “fewer than 400” of them had voted and that it has begun replacing the vendor involved in the improper registrations.</p><p>Pennsylvania's secretary of the commonwealth, Republican Al Schmidt, said in a letter this week that DHS officials acknowledged during a recent meeting they did not have high confidence that the 14,576 people referenced in the initial letter were in fact noncitizens improperly registered to vote. He said federal officials said they would provide a methodology and that Pennsylvania officials were awaiting that information.</p><p>Nevada Secretary of State Francisco Aguilar, a Democrat, said he did not understand the methodology the federal government used.</p><p>“All I can say is we have done significant work to make sure our voter rolls are as clean as possible,” he said.</p><p>Messages from The Associated Press seeking comment from DHS were not immediately returned.</p><h4>Tightening election security or interfering in the midterms?</h4><p>The relentless attention on claims that noncitizens are marring elections in the United States comes as Trump continues to pressure Republican senators to <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/save-america-act-senate-recess-6dd2d8084ee42653b4db79cd565d1504" target="_blank" >pass a bill</a> that would require people to show documented proof of American citizenship when they register to vote for the midterms, even though millions of people <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/save-act-documents-requirements-citizenship-voting-congress-dfb43bcdd0255d3665da588a60286b4e" target="_blank" >do not have ready access</a> to such records.</p><p>The Safeguard American Voter Eligibility, or SAVE America Act, has passed the GOP-led House but is stalled in the Senate, where even some members of the president's party are skeptical of its provisions.</p><p>Kathy Boockvar, former Democratic secretary of state of Pennsylvania who now runs a nonpartisan election security firm, said she viewed the administration's release of the census report as part of a “doing everything it can” strategy to pass the legislation.</p><p>Republican supporters say the bill would improve the integrity of elections, including the requirement to show a photo ID. Gathering the documents necessary to prove citizenship would be difficult for many would-be voters. A 2025 University of Maryland study estimates that <a class="Link" href="https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/Who%20Lacks%20Documentary%20Proof%20of%20Citizenship%20March%202025.pdf" target="_blank" >21.3 million people</a> in the U.S. who are eligible to vote do not have, or do not have easy access to, documents proving their citizenship.</p><p>Trump's opponents say his raising the specter of noncitizens voting leading to fraudulent results is less about maintaining the integrity of elections than it is about him doing whatever he can so his party retains power in Washington after November.</p><p>On Friday, the U.S. attorney's office in Los Angeles used the arrest of a Honduran national on charges alleging he fraudulently registered to vote as a signal that more attention on the issue was coming for California, a state that has a handful of important U.S. House races in November. Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said the arrest was “the first of many to come” while warning “there’s no telling how many noncitizens are currently registered to vote” in the state.</p><p>“Trump is trying to lay the groundwork to reject the ’26 election,” said Colorado's secretary of state, Democrat Jena Griswold. “He’s trying to destabilize both confidence and actual election administration. His efforts to destabilize election information, administration are not working.”</p>
